title: How to Manage a Business Blog: Tools for Planning, Writing, and Publishing
excerpt: A business blog only works if you can run it consistently. Here are the tools Kenyan businesses need to plan, write, publish, and measure posts.
author: Noon Studio Africa

content.text: You can run a serious business blog with a Google Sheet, Google Docs, and a content management system that costs nothing extra. The toolchain does not need to be expensive; it needs to cover four jobs: planning, writing, publishing, and measuring. Most blogs die not from bad writing but from a messy process.
This guide walks through each job, the tools that do it well, and the workflow we use with Kenyan clients. You will see exactly what to set up and what to skip.

content.text: The Four Jobs of a Business Blog

Every blog, from a Nairobi bakery to a Kampala software firm, runs on the same four jobs: planning what to write, writing and editing it, publishing it, and measuring what happened. If any job is missing, the blog stalls.

The mistake most businesses make is buying a fancy tool for one job and ignoring the other three. A beautiful CMS with no calendar produces nothing. A great calendar with no analytics produces guesswork.
Why Kenyan Business Blogs Stall

In our experience, the reason Kenyan business blogs go quiet is process, not talent. The founder writes three posts, gets busy, and the blog stops. There is no queue of drafted work and no scheduled dates to protect.

A toolchain fixes this by making the next step obvious. When a post is drafted, it moves to editing. When it is edited, it is scheduled. When it is published, it is measured. Nobody has to remember what comes next.
Mobile access matters too. Many Kenyan business owners manage their blog from a phone between meetings, so pick tools with decent phone apps or at least a usable mobile web version.
Planning: The Content Calendar
The calendar is the engine room. Notion and Google Sheets are the two most common choices we see:

items: Google Sheets: free, familiar, and shareable with a small team
Notion: a proper database with statuses, filters, and a calendar view

content.text: Keep columns for title, keyword, status, publish date, and author. Plan one month ahead at minimum, and batch topics by theme so writing sessions stay focused. A calendar that lives in someone's head is not a calendar.
One habit worth stealing: review the calendar with the team for ten minutes every Monday. It takes almost no time and it keeps the pipeline honest.
Writing and Editing
Google Docs is the workhorse for drafting: comments, suggestions, and version history make editing painless. Grammarly catches the obvious errors before a human has to.

If you use AI for drafts, treat it as a junior writer. It produces a competent first version; a human adds the voice, the local examples, and the final judgment. Publish AI text untouched and readers will feel it.
Whatever tool you choose for drafting, keep every post in the same place. A single folder beats a trail of documents scattered across email, chat, and drives.
Keep a short style guide in the same folder as your calendar: tone, banned words, how you address the reader. It keeps every post sounding like the same brand.
Publishing: The Content Management System
The CMS is where posts go live. The right choice depends on who runs the blog day to day:

rows: Huge ecosystem, SEO plugins, scheduled publishing
Teams that want a clean writing experience
Custom site on a modern stack
Businesses that want zero dashboard maintenance

content.text: WordPress powers a large share of business blogs and handles SEO and scheduling out of the box. A custom site publishes with a simple push and needs no dashboard to babysit. Choose based on who will do the daily work.
Scheduling and Distribution

Scheduling turns finished posts into a reliable stream. Buffer and Hootsuite schedule social posts in advance. Meta Business Suite does it free for Facebook and Instagram. Mailchimp or Substack turns each post into an email newsletter.

items: Write one week ahead and schedule the next
Turn each post into three social snippets
Send the newsletter the day the post goes live

content.text: In Kenya, do not forget WhatsApp. A status update pointing to the new post reaches customers who never open email.
Images
Canva handles graphics and keeps brand templates consistent. Pexels and Pixabay supply free stock photos. Keep a folder of brand templates so every post image looks like the same business.
One tip we give every client: design the social image at the same time as the post. It takes five minutes and saves a frantic search on publish day.
Measuring
Google Analytics 4 shows which posts bring traffic. Google Search Console shows which keywords you rank for. Check both once a month, then write more of what works.
We also ask clients to track the boring numbers: enquiries, calls, and WhatsApp messages that mention the blog. That link between content and revenue is what keeps the blog funded.

Do not obsess over daily numbers. A monthly review is enough: which posts earned traffic, which keywords moved, and which topics deserve a follow-up. Small data over a long time beats big data looked at once.
The Workflow We Use With Clients
Tools only help if the process is clear. Here is the weekly rhythm we set up with Kenyan clients:

items: Monday: review the calendar for the next two weeks and pick the next post.
Tuesday: write the first draft from the queue, using the style guide.
Wednesday: edit, add images, and schedule the post.
Thursday: answer comments and share the post in relevant groups.
Friday: publish, distribute on social and WhatsApp, and log the metrics.

content.text: That is roughly four focused hours a week, and it keeps the blog weeks ahead of its publish dates. The rhythm matters more than any single tool.
If Friday publishing feels stressful, move it to Thursday. The day matters less than the fact that it happens every week, without exception.
You will notice the same four jobs inside the rhythm: planning on Monday, writing on Tuesday, publishing midweek, and measuring on Friday. The tools simply support the loop.
Common Blog Management Mistakes

items: Buying a tool before building a process
Planning without scheduling, so posts depend on memory
Letting drafts pile up in email and chat instead of one folder
Publishing without images or with inconsistent branding
Measuring likes instead of traffic, enquiries, and rankings
Stopping the moment the founder gets busy

FAQ

items.q: What is the best tool to manage a business blog?
items.a: There is no single best tool. Use Google Sheets for planning, Google Docs for writing, and WordPress or Ghost for publishing. The combination matters more than any one product.

items.q: How much does blog management cost in Kenya?
items.a: The tools can cost nothing: Sheets, Docs, and Meta Business Suite are free. Paid plans for Notion, Buffer, or Mailchimp run a few thousand shillings a month. If you outsource the writing, budget from KES 15,000 per post.

items.q: Should I use AI to write my blog posts?
items.a: Use it for drafts and outlines, then have a human rewrite and localize. AI lacks your voice and your customer knowledge. A Nairobi reader can tell the difference instantly.

items.q: How often should a business publish blog posts?
items.a: Once a week is a sustainable target for most small businesses, twice a week if you have a dedicated writer. The rhythm matters more than the volume.
